title: Capacity curve playback weekly sync
summary: Weekly POC check-in to review throughput curves from the past week of traffic replay, discuss continuous batching and queueing adjustments, validate concurrency targets for 99th percentile latency, and align on next steps for burst capacity and billing. Main takeaways: steady-state throughput improved with smaller batch caps, tail latency still spikes on long-context requests, plan to trial aggressive prefix KV cache for chat flows and add a small reserved burst for peak windows.
topics: Tail latency causes (long context / token gen)
Burst capacity and fallback model strategy

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-04 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Mei Tang (Redwood SE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood CSM); Jordan Lee (QuantaMed Eng Lead), Priya Shah (SRE), Samir Patel (Product), Lena Ortiz (Data)

Summary (auto): weekly playback review, tuning batch/concurrency, next steps captured.

00:00 Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. we were going to start by going over the playback from the last 48 hours. Mei has the numbers.
00:18 Mei: yeah so I uploaded the playback csv to the shared drive, link in the notes, but top line — steady state throughput increased about 12% after the smaller batch cap change we rolled monday night. however, we see tail latency spikes still when the sequences go beyond ~4k tokens, looks like kv cache misses and repeated prefix recompute.
00:40 Jordan: can you remind me which model variant we ran for that run? was it the 7B q4 with quantization?
00:47 Mei: correct, we used rwd-7b-q4v2, we also had the fallback to rwd-6b-lite for the small dev traffic. there might be a mismatch in memory layout causing some extra memcpy overhead, the trace shows several context swap points.
01:05 Priya: when you say "tail spikes", are those transient 99.9% weird ones or sustained 99th percentile? because our SLAs care about 99th more than average.
01:15 Mei: most are 99th/99.9th. the 99th is often within target except when a batch contains a mixture of short and very long requests; the longer ones push the batch out and you hit backpressure and queue growth.
01:30 Samir: so that suggests we need better request shaping on client side or change how you batch. what are our knob options again?
01:36 Mei: we can change max_batch_tokens, batch_timeout_ms, and also split by predicted sequence length to avoid mixing. continuous batching also supports a per-route concurrency cap so we don't over-commit GPUs.
01:50 Jordan: we don't really have reliable predicted length in prod yet, we do have a predict pipeline in kafka that could add an estimate but it's a bit late to ship. is there a simpler config?
02:02 Mei: simplest is to set a lower max_batch_tokens so the long ones don't hold up the slot. we tried 4096 -> 2048 and saw throughput up while tail drops by about 10-15% on the 99th. trade is slightly higher CPU overhead due to more batches.
02:20 Alex: cost tradeoff there. Mei, do you have an approximate tokens-per-second delta so we can quantify $$ impact?
02:26 Mei: ballpark — throughput increased 12%, token cost per million reduced by about 6% because batching efficiency improved. but GPU occupancy goes up and longer-run cost may tick. I'll add the numbers to the spreadsheet.
02:40 Lena: is KV cache prefixing something we can enable? it sounds promising for chat flows where users have long histories.
02:46 Mei: yes, the pilot supports prefix KV cache. It helps when you have repeated prefixes across requests. the caveat is memory growth on the host and slightly more complex eviction logic. we enabled a conservative TTL for the pilot run.
03:00 Jordan: what about concurrency targets? we set our customer-side concurrency at 16 but we're still seeing queue depth occasionally at 45.
03:09 Mei: that's queue depth across the whole pool. policy routing is allowing bursts from a few clients; we can set per-customer concurrency caps in the routing layer or do a soft rate shape.
03:20 Priya: that's important. we need an upper bound to prevent noisy neighbors. we also need audit logs for who made what calls when — compliance requires that.
03:30 Daniel (CSM): we can provide audit-log export, Alex will follow up on the retention and S3 bucket.
03:38 Alex: yep, will share the S3 link and retention policy.
03:40 Samir: Any sign of inconsistent behavior across regions? we had one spike yesterday in eu-west that didn't show in us-west.
03:49 Mei: that was due to a small kernel selection mismatch - the runtime chose a slower matmul path for that pod. we patched the kernel selector and rebalanced. should be stable now.
04:00 Jordan: ok good. can we try the new batch cap and prefix KV and run a focused 24h playback that includes our 50 long-context prompt samples?
04:08 Mei: yes. if you share the samples we'll include them in the trace.
04:12 Jordan: I'll drop them in the drive later today.
04:15 Alex: for pricing, we'll propose a burst capacity add-on that can be called for predictable windows, you'll be billed for reserved slots and overage. we'll show an estimate.
04:26 Priya: on security items — we need to see the SOC2 report and confirm KMS rotation. also SSO (SAML) for access.
04:33 Alex: we have SOC2 type II, will share PDF. KMS integration supported with customer-managed keys, rotation doc in the security folder. SAML SSO is in the roadmap but we can provide SCIM provisioning token for now.
04:44 Jordan: great. on fallback mapping: when GPU capacity is constrained do you fall back to a smaller model or to a CPU path? what's the latency delta?
04:53 Mei: we fall back to a smaller GPU-optimized variant first; CPU fallback is only for very low priority tasks. fallback to smaller model increases per-request latency 80-120ms but keeps p95/p99 within acceptable bounds; cost drops roughly 30% depending on model family.
05:10 Samir: competitors like Anthropic have similar fallback approaches — any reason to prefer yours?
05:16 Alex: we think our routing + KV cache + continuous batching mix gives better steady-state cost/latency tradeoffs and clearer observability for per-token costs. also rollouts and canary policies are first-class which helps enterprise risk reduction.
05:30 Mei: quick note — i saw some transcription artifacts in the logs we pulled, sometimes service names get munged (eg K-V cache vs KVcach), so pls ignore that noise in the csv.
05:40 Jordan: fair. let's capture explicit next steps.
05:43 Alex: recap — Mei will deploy batch cap change and KV prefix, run 24h playback; Jordan will share long-context bundle; Priya to confirm audit-log export location; Alex to send pricing/burst option and SOC2 doc. We'll reconvene next tuesday same time to review playback.
06:00 Priya: one more question — will enabling prefix KV change data residency or memory-sensitive compliance flags?
06:10 Mei: it doesn't move customer data outside their region; KV stays in the VPC for private pilots. memory footprint increases but we can set TTLs and caps per-namespace.
06:22 Jordan: thanks all. that's it from me.
06:25 Alex: thanks, we'll follow up in email with links. meeting adjourned.
